summary: Describes a reference model for Autonomic Networking in managed networks. It defines how an autonomic node behaves, how the elements of an autonomic context work together, and how autonomic services can use the infrastructure.

plainLanguage.summary: A blueprint of how a self-managing network is put together and how its parts cooperate.

questions: what is the autonomic control plane
subtitle: A blueprint for self-managing networks that operate with minimal human intervention.

tldr.problem: Enterprise and carrier networks require constant manual configuration and monitoring. As networks grow and change, skilled operators struggle to manage complexity, provisioning, and fault recovery efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: Autonomic Networking provides a reference model where network nodes automatically coordinate, discover neighbors, establish secure channels, and run distributed functions called Autonomic Service Agents. The infrastructure includes a secure control plane, trust relationships based on PKI, and mechanisms for nodes to negotiate and synchronize without human direction.
tldr.outcome: Networks can self-manage routine operations like enrollment, recovery, and optimization while humans provide only high-level intent. This model is designed for professionally managed networks where operator oversight remains important.

facts.label: Trust model
facts.value: PKI with CA, registrars, and MASA

facts.label: Mandatory ASAs
facts.value: Pledge, Join Proxy, ACP, and others

today: RFC 8993 is an Informational document that provides the reference model for Autonomic Networking. It describes the Phase 1 architecture, with some topics (marked with *) identified as areas for future work beyond the current implementation scope. The model is the foundation for the Standards Track specifications in RFCs 8990 (GRASP), 8994 (ACP), and 8995 (BRSKI).

sections.title: What Autonomic Networking Means
sections.content:
Autonomic Networking aims to reduce operational burden by enabling networks to self-manage, self-optimize, and self-heal. Rather than configuring each device individually, operators set high-level Intent describing what the network should do. The network infrastructure then translates Intent into device-specific actions.

This reference model applies to professionally managed networks (such as enterprise or carrier networks) where skilled operators oversee the system, rather than unmanaged networks. The model is designed to coexist with traditional management: some functions can be autonomic while others remain manually configured.

For example, in an existing non-autonomic network, operators could use the trust infrastructure described in this model to establish security certificates on all devices. Once trust is in place, they could then bring up an Autonomic Control Plane for secure communication and run autonomic functions on top of it.
sections.plainLanguage: A network that manages itself using a blueprint that lets devices coordinate automatically, with human experts setting only the top-level goals.

sections.title: Node and Infrastructure Architecture
sections.content:
The model defines two layers within each autonomic node. The Autonomic Networking Infrastructure (ANI) is a foundation that all nodes implement, providing basic services like naming, addressing, discovery, and routing. Above the ANI, Autonomic Service Agents (ASAs) implement specific functions: one ASA might handle device enrollment, another handles link optimization, and so on.

Each node maintains an adjacency table containing information about neighboring nodes: their IP addresses, domain membership, and certificates. This table is populated by link-local discovery (using IPv6 link-local addresses autonomically), vendor redirects, and manual configuration if needed. The adjacency table drives the node's behavior: when a node discovers neighbors in the same domain with valid certificates, it can authenticate them and establish an Autonomic Control Plane (ACP) channel.

The ACP is a secure overlay network where all control traffic flows. It is built hop-by-hop on top of the data plane, using cryptographic authentication and encryption. Once a node joins the ACP, it can discover services (such as registrars for enrollment), run distributed functions, and receive Intent from a central policy source.
sections.plainLanguage: Each device has a foundation layer that handles the basics (who are my neighbors, how do I talk securely) and upper layers that run specific functions like enrollment or optimization.

sections.title: The Node Lifecycle
sections.content:
An autonomic node follows a state machine with three states, persisting across power cycles through a stored domain identity called the Local Device Identifier (LDevID).

Factory Default: A new device leaves the factory with only a vendor-provided identifier (IDevID). It has no domain-specific configuration. When powered on, it begins discovery and attempts to bootstrap into a domain by finding neighbors and requesting enrollment.

Enrolled: After successful enrollment, the device has an LDevID proving its membership in a domain. However, it may not yet have an ACP channel (perhaps no neighbors are in the domain yet). The device remains responsive to bootstrap requests from new devices and waits to join the ACP when possible.

In ACP: Once at least one ACP channel to another domain node is established, the device can participate in full autonomic operations. It can now discover services via GRASP (a protocol for negotiation and discovery inside the ACP), run ASAs, and receive Intent distribution. If the last ACP channel drops, the device returns to Enrolled state.

A factory reset removes the LDevID and returns the device to Factory Default state, erasing all domain-specific configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: A device starts new, enrolls itself in a domain once it finds neighbors, then joins the secure control network to participate in the domain's autonomic functions.

sections.title: Security and Trust Infrastructure
sections.content:
Autonomic Networking is self-protecting: all protocols are secure by default without requiring administrators to explicitly configure security, except for establishing a PKI infrastructure.

The model uses a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) with a Certification Authority (CA) and registrars acting as Registration Authorities. Each domain has one or more registrars that issue domain certificates (LDevIDs). A Manufacturer Authorized Signing Authority (MASA), operated by device vendors, provides ownership tracking and assists in bootstrap by issuing audit and authorization tokens.

New devices use their IDevID (a certificate pre-installed by the manufacturer) to authenticate themselves during enrollment. The MASA can confirm that the device is legitimate and has not been previously enrolled elsewhere. Once authenticated, the registrar issues an LDevID specific to the domain.

In the current phase, devices within a domain are either fully trusted (they have valid domain certificates) or fully untrusted (they do not). Future phases may introduce subdomains with partial trust relationships.
sections.plainLanguage: New devices prove they are real using a manufacturer-provided certificate, and the network's trust center issues them a domain certificate. From then on, they can prove membership and talk securely to other domain devices.

sections.title: Autonomic Service Agents and Management
sections.content:
Autonomic Service Agents (ASAs) are processes running on autonomic nodes that implement autonomic functions. Infrastructure ASAs are mandatory on all nodes: the pledge ASA (for enrollment), join proxy ASA (helping other devices enroll), and ACP ASA (establishing the control plane). Other ASAs are optional and implement domain-specific functions like optimization or monitoring.

ASAs discover each other and negotiate using GRASP (GeneRic Autonomic Signaling Protocol), a protocol that runs both in the data plane during bootstrap and inside the ACP during normal operation. GRASP allows ASAs to exchange complex technical objectives and reach agreement on parameters.

Networks typically run some autonomic functions alongside traditional management. A conflict resolution hierarchy ensures that manual configuration has the highest priority, followed by autonomic Intent (medium priority), and finally autonomic default behavior (lowest priority). This allows operators to override autonomic decisions when needed.

Intent is a high-level policy distributed throughout the domain, describing what the network should achieve. Intent changes infrequently (on the order of days) and is flooded to all nodes. ASAs use Intent to guide their behavior while maintaining self-awareness of their node's capabilities and the surrounding network topology.
sections.plainLanguage: Software agents on each device handle enrollment, secure communication, and domain-specific tasks. They coordinate using a negotiation protocol and follow high-level policies set by operators.
